title: SHARAVAN OBERAI versus STATE OF UTTARAKHAND

paras.text:
UKHC010156522026
2026:UHC:8551
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Misc Application No. 1937 of 2026
16 September, 2026
Sharavan Oberai --Applicant
Versus
State Of Uttarakhand and another --Respondents
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Presence:-
Mr. Arvind Vashistha, learned Senior counsel assisted by Ms.Disha
Vashistha, learned counsel for applicant.
Mr. Chitrarth Kandpal, learned Brief Holder for the State of
Uttarakhand/respondent No.1.
Mr. Rajat Mittal and Mr. Rishabh Rangar, learned counsel for
respondent no.2.
Hon'ble Pankaj Purohit, J. (Oral)
The present application under Section 528 of
the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 has been
filed by the applicant seeking quashing of the charge-sheet No. 01 dated 13.09.2025 and supplementary
charge-sheet No. 02 dated 10.11.2025, arising out of FIR
No. 510 of 2024, under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471 and
120-B of the Indian Penal Code, Police Station Kotwali
Nagar, District Dehradun, as well as the
cognizance/summoning order dated 12.06.2026 passed
by the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Dehradun in
Criminal Case No. 3776 of 2026, whereby cognizance has
been taken against the applicant for the aforesaid
offences.
2. The facts of the case are that the property in
question, bearing Khasra No. 235 Kha (old Khasra No.
359/2), situated at Mauza Kuanwala, District Dehradun,
was owned by co-accused Amrish Kumar Oberai and was
mortgaged with Union Bank of India. In the year 2017,
the first informant Shashank Kumar and others agreed
1

UKHC010156522026
2026:UHC:8551
to purchase the property for a consideration of
₹1,26,50,000/-. The consideration was paid through
banking channels and a registered sale deed was
executed in their favour on 15th March, 2018. It is alleged
that despite the subsisting mortgage, the vendors
represented in the sale deed that the property was free
from all encumbrances, mortgage, debt and litigation
and, on the basis of such misrepresentation, induced the
purchasers to part with the sale consideration. It is
further alleged that a forged revenue record was prepared
and used in connection with the transaction.
3. Subsequently, the property was auctioned by
Union Bank of India on 26.07.2019 and was purchased
by Udit Goenka, who thereafter sold the same to
Shashank Kumar and Shobhit Kumar by registered sale
deed dated 15.06.2020. On an application under Section
175(3) BNSS, FIR No. 510 of 2024 was registered on
28.11.2024 under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471 and 120-
B IPC. After investigation, charge-sheet dated 13.09.2025
and supplementary charge-sheet dated 10.11.2025 were
submitted, whereafter the learned Chief Judicial
Magistrate, Dehradun, vide order dated 12.06.2026, took
cognizance and summoned the applicant. Hence, the
present application.
4. Learned counsel for the applicant submits that
the entire prosecution is an abuse of the process of law,
as the dispute essentially arises out of a commercial
transaction relating to the sale of the property in
question. It is submitted that the property was
admittedly mortgaged with Union Bank of India and the
purchasers were aware of the subsisting mortgage and
the One Time Settlement proceedings with the Bank. The
2

UKHC010156522026
2026:UHC:8551
transaction was entered into through registered
documents and the entire sale consideration of
₹1,26,50,000/- was paid through banking channels. It is,
therefore, contended that the dispute, at its highest,
relates to the title and encumbrance over the property
and recovery of money, for which the parties have already
pursued civil and proceedings under Section 138 of the
Negotiable Instruments Act.
5. Learned counsel for the applicant further
submits that the purchasers subsequently acquired
complete knowledge of the mortgage and the Bank's
proceedings and, after the property was auctioned by the
Bank, themselves purchased the same property from the
auction purchaser by registered sale deed dated
15.06.2020 for ₹2,75,00,000/-. Despite such knowledge,
the criminal proceedings were initiated only in the year
2024. It is argued that this subsequent conduct of the
purchasers, coupled with the considerable delay in
lodging the FIR, demonstrates that the criminal
proceedings have been initiated as a means of exerting
pressure for recovery of money.
6. It is further submitted by the learned counsel
for the applicant that the essential ingredients of
cheating are absent, as there was no dishonest intention
on the part of the applicant at the inception of the
transaction. The property was admittedly owned by the
vendors, the sale was effected through a registered
instrument and the consideration was paid through
banking channels. Learned counsel submits that the
allegation regarding the forged revenue record is also
wholly untenable, as there is no material to show that
the applicant prepared, fabricated or altered the said
3

UKHC010156522026
2026:UHC:8551
document. The revenue record was maintained by the
competent revenue authorities and the applicant cannot
be held responsible merely on the basis of its alleged use
in the transaction.
7. Learned counsel for the applicant also submits
that the material collected during investigation itself
contains the statements of the concerned persons under
Section 180 of BNSS, 2023, indicating that the
purchasers had been informed about the mortgage and
the settlement proceedings with the Bank. It is, therefore,
argued that the very foundation of the allegation of
dishonest concealment is contradicted by the prosecution
material itself. Learned counsel submits that the learned
Magistrate has taken cognizance mechanically without
properly examining whether the essential ingredients of
Sections 420, 467, 468, 471 and 120-B IPC are made out
against the applicant. On these grounds, it is urged that
the charge-sheets, the order taking cognizance and the
consequential criminal proceedings against the applicant
deserve to be quashed.
8. Per contra, learned State counsel as well as
learned counsel for respondent no.2 submit that the
material collected during investigation discloses a prima
facie case against the applicant and the defence raised by
him involves disputed questions of fact. It is further
submitted that the subsequent knowledge of the
purchasers regarding the mortgage and the
circumstances relied upon by the applicant are matters
to be appreciated during trial and cannot be conclusively
examined in proceedings under Section 528 BNSS. The
sale-deed dated 15.03.2018 contained a clear recital that
the land is free from all encumbrances and mortgage etc.
4

UKHC010156522026
2026:UHC:8551
Thus statement of mediator Shri Vijay Singh Parmar
under Section 180 of BNSS, 2023 is contrary to record.
The fact of mortgage should have been mentioned clearly
in the sale-deed dated 15.03.2018. Hence, no
interference is warranted and the application deserves to
be dismissed.
9. Heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the material on record, the principal defence of
the applicant is that the purchasers were aware of the
subsisting mortgage and the One Time Settlement
proceedings with Union Bank of India and, therefore,
there was no dishonest intention on his part. It is further
contended that the dispute is essentially civil in nature.
However, while exercising jurisdiction under Section 528
BNSS, this Court is not required to appreciate evidence
or adjudicate disputed questions of fact, but only to
examine whether the allegations, taken at their face
value, disclose the ingredients of the offences alleged.
10. The registered sale deed dated 15.03.2018
contains a categorical recital that the property was free
from mortgage, encumbrance, debt and litigation,
whereas the prosecution case is that the property was, in
fact, mortgaged with Union Bank of India and such
misrepresentation was made to induce the purchasers to
part with ₹1,26,50,000/-. Thus, the allegations, taken at
their face value, prima facie disclose the ingredients of
cheating. The subsequent sale deed dated 15.06.2020
and the alleged knowledge of the purchasers regarding
the mortgage do not conclusively establish their
knowledge at the time of the original transaction.
11. The statements of Shashank Kumar and
Shobhit Kumar recorded under Section 180 BNSS,
5

UKHC010156522026
2026:UHC:8551
forming part of the investigation material, contain
allegations that the vendors represented the property to
be free from encumbrance and that the mortgage came to
their knowledge subsequently. The evidentiary value of
these statements and the applicant's contrary version are
matters to be tested at trial. Mediator Shri Vijay Singh
Parmar's statement under Section 180 of BNSS, 2023 are
contrary to the recital made in sale-deed dated
15.03.2018 (Annexure No.1 to the application). The fact
of mortgage shall be mentioned in the sale-deed for
clarity.
12. As regards the alleged forged revenue record,
whether it was forged, knowingly used as genuine and
what role is attributable to the applicant also require
appreciation of evidence. The mere availability of civil
remedies or proceedings under the Negotiable
Instruments Act would not, by itself, warrant quashing
where the allegations prima facie disclose criminal
offences.
13. On an overall consideration, this Court finds
that the applicant essentially seeks adjudication of his
defence, which is beyond the limited scope of jurisdiction
under Section 528 BNSS. No ground for interference with
the charge-sheets, the order taking cognizance or the
consequential proceedings is made out.
14. Accordingly, this C 528 application is dismissed.
 (Pankaj Purohit, J.)
 16.09.2026
Nahid
